data.title: Sporotrichosis — viva
data.summary: Fungal infections · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Sporotrichosis** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. What is sporotrichosis? Agent?**
- Subacute/chronic subcutaneous mycosis caused by the thermally dimorphic Sporothrix schenckii complex (S. schenckii, S. brasiliensis, S. globosa — commonest in Asia/India)
- Mould in environment (25 °C), yeast in tissue (37 °C)

**Q2. How is it acquired and who gets it?**
- Implantation from soil, plants, thorns (rose — 'rose gardener's disease'), sphagnum moss, hay, wood splinters; zoonotic from cat scratches (S. brasiliensis — Brazil epidemic)
- Gardeners, farmers, florists, forestry workers; in India — sub-Himalayan belt (Himachal, north-east, Uttarakhand), Kangra valley

**Q3. Describe the clinical types.**
- Lymphocutaneous (~75%): papulonodule at inoculation site (hand/forearm) ulcerates (sporotrichoid chancre) → secondary nodules along the lymphatic chain ascending the limb
- Fixed cutaneous: single plaque/verrucous/ulcerated lesion without lymphatic spread — common on face in children in endemic areas (more immune host)
- Disseminated cutaneous and systemic (osteoarticular, pulmonary — inhalation, meningeal) in immunosuppressed (HIV, alcoholism, diabetes)

**Q4. What is the sporotrichoid pattern and its differentials?**
- Nodules in a linear chain along lymphatics
- Causes: sporotrichosis, Mycobacterium marinum (fish-tank granuloma), Nocardia brasiliensis, leishmaniasis (L. braziliensis), tularaemia, cat-scratch disease, other mycobacteria, blastomycosis — remember 'SLNM'

**Q5. How do you investigate?**
- Histopathology: pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, mixed suppurative granuloma ('sporotrichoid granuloma' with central neutrophils, middle histiocytes, outer lymphocytes); organisms scanty — small cigar-shaped yeasts, asteroid bodies (Splendore–Hoeppli) with PAS/GMS
- Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25 °C — the gold standard (moist white colonies becoming dark; sleeve/flower-like conidia); conversion to yeast at 37 °C
- PCR; sporotrichin skin test (epidemiology)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Itraconazole 100–200 mg/day (drug of choice) — continue 2–4 weeks after lesions resolve (usually 3–6 months)
- Saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI): start 5 drops thrice daily increased to 40–50 drops thrice daily — cheap and effective in India; side effects: metallic taste, salivary gland swelling, acneiform rash, GI upset, hypothyroidism; avoid in pregnancy
- Terbinafine 250–500 mg/day alternative; local hyperthermia (warm compresses) as adjunct — fungus does not grow above 37 °C
- Amphotericin B for disseminated/pulmonary/meningeal disease, then itraconazole

**Q7. Differential diagnosis of fixed cutaneous sporotrichosis.**
- Lupus vulgaris, TBVC, chromoblastomycosis, leishmaniasis, pyoderma, blastomycosis, SCC, atypical mycobacterial infection

**Q8. Why is the fixed type common on the face of children?**
- Repeated exposure in endemic areas produces strong immunity, which limits lymphatic spread

**Q9. What is an asteroid body?**
- Central yeast surrounded by radiating eosinophilic Splendore–Hoeppli material — seen in sporotrichosis (also sarcoidosis has 'asteroid bodies' of a different kind inside giant cells)

**Q10. Which drug is used in pregnancy?**
- Avoid azoles and iodides; local heat therapy; amphotericin B for severe disease

## Quick spotter facts
- Ascending nodules along lymphatics from a hand ulcer — sporotrichosis
- SSKI — cheap drug that works
- Asteroid bodies

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 19A (Subcutaneous mycoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
